subsubtopic: ATLANTIC CANADA-OPPOSITION TO ELIMINATION OF PASSENGER SERVICE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Atlantic Canadians and specifically Prince Edward Islanders will not accept the Tories' agenda of making the rich richer and the poor poorer. The proposed elimination of VIA passenger service is one of the many examples of this agenda.
The constituents of my riding of Hillsborough know what it is like to be cut off from passenger train service. Why? Because we do not have such a service. We have to hop a bus and travel to Moncton. The only tracks left in our red soil are left by the people dragging their feet to the VIA bus.
Aside from the passenger train service, there will be direct and indirect damage done if VIA Rail is canned. Think of the effect on our highways and our tourist industry, and what about the 7,500 Canadians directly employed by VIA Rail? If other industrialized countries can successfully operate such a transportation service, then surely Canada can as well.

Mr. Speaker, there are only two sources of human food. One is water and the other is soil. Unlike the civilizations of old such as those along the Tigris and Euphrates Rivers, humanity no longer has the option of relocating after it has destroyed its food-producing resources.
One of the great myths of Canadian society is the commonly-held belief that we have an abundance of agricultural land. We do not. Only 7 per cent of Canada's land mass, situated in climatically favourably areas, has been deemed agricultural. Moreover, a very large percentage of Canada's original agricultural land has now been permanently destroyed. More than 50 per cent of the original farmland of Ontario is lost to urban sprawl and transport systems. On the prairies, vast regions of once productive lands are now marginal or barren because of erosion or degradation.
I want to salute the initiative of the Minister of Agriculture to have a task force to consider new and appropriate approaches to soil conservation and crop management. May this process bring about a greater respect for our soils and the need for their conservation and enrichment.

subsubtopic: NATIONAL LIFE ENRICHED BY WORK OF VOLUNTEERS
speechtext:
As this is National Volunteer Week, I would like to express most sincere thanks to the millions of people across this country who devote their time and talents to voluntary service. I speak not only on behalf of myself and all my parliamentary colleagues but also for all Canadians who take such fervent pride in our tradition of service to others.
Volunteers are men and women from all walks of life. They are retired, employed, homemakers and students- people from diverse socio-economic backgrounds, people from all religious, racial and culture groupings-Canadians both young and young at heart.
Canada's volunteers play a strong and vital role in our national life. They deliver much-needed human and social services, they champion worthy causes, and they simply make things happen. Volunteers serve on community and citizen action committees and on the boards of volunteer organizations. They place the needs of others before their own. Thanks to them, a stranger becomes a neighbour and a neighbour is more like a friend. All Canadians owe a debt of gratitude to our volunteers,

April 12, 1989
and we, the Members of this House, are honoured to pay tribute to them.

Mr. Speaker Canadian policy on international development assistance is to link aid to a country's human rights record. Since 1983, Canada has provided over $13 million in bilateral aid to the Government of El Salvador.
With the presidential elections concluded, government-supported violence and repression are on the increase. Last week, Christina Gomez, a Salvadoran leader of the Women's Popular Movement and mother of four, was abducted by heavily-armed men and summarily executed.
Canadians do not want to be associated with a regime which utilizes human rights violations and murder. Canadians are proud of our record of promoting peace, yet our Government, through bilateral aid, does business with this Government which refuses to negotiate a settlement to the nine-year war.
There are dozens of non-governmental organizations promoting peace and the necessary social reform to ensure peace. I call on the Government to reconsider our bilateral aid program to El Salvador so that the aid is channeled through non-governmental organizations until we see a substantial improvement in the human rights environment.

subtopic: THE HONOURABLE ROBERT C. COATES APPOINTMENT AS HONORARY CHIEF OF MICMAC INDIAN BAND
THE HONOURABLE ROBERT C. COATES APPOINTMENT AS HONORARY CHIEF OF MICMAC INDIAN BAND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to pay tribute to a former Member of this House who served here faithfully for 31 years. Of course, I am referring to my predecessor, the Hon. Robert C. Coates, and I am pleased to announce that on April 7, Bob was given a very unique honour by Chief Lawrence Paul of the Micmac band in Millbrook near Truro, Nova Scotia.
Bob was made an honorary chief in a very moving ceremony conducted by the band medicine man. This honour is even more significant when one realizes it has never been awarded to anyone before. The new name bestowed on Bob kind of says it all. They have named him "The Chief Who Kept Many Promises", and this title is indicative of the feelings of the constituents of our riding and at least partly explains why he was elected for 11 consecutive terms.
I do not know if protocol calls for him to be referred to as Chief Hon. Bob or Hon. Chief Bob, but whatever it is, it will probably be just plain old Bob to the rest of us. I know you will all join me in congratulating Chief Bob and wishing him good luck in any future opportunities that may present themselves.

Mr. Francis G. LeBlanc (Cape Breton Highlands-
Canso): Mr. Speaker, many people in my constituency of Cape Breton Highlands-Canso and elsewhere in Canada are deeply distressed that for more than than 14 months there has been abortion on demand in Canada. I share their concerns.
Legislation to protect the unborn in Canada and to fill the void left by the Supreme Court decision of January 28, 1988, is an urgent necessity and is long overdue. The Government's feeble undertaking to study the implications of the Supreme Court jurisprudence is just not good enough. There has been ample time for study. The time now is for action, and action means the speedy introduction of a Bill that reconciles the legitimate right of the mother with protection for the unborn from conception onwards.
The Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) promised during the Leaders' debates prior to the election that legislation would be introduced upon the return of the House. I urge the Prime Minister to keep his promise to Canadians and indicate to this House when we can expect to consider this important matter.
April 12, 1989

Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mrs. McDougall) unveiled yesterday the government proposals for unemployment insurance reform. Thousands of Canadians across the nation were both surprised and stunned by the news. But for millions of others, it was a clear indication that the government wants to remedy abuses.
Who hasn't heard, at one time or another, of some people who quit their jobs for no reason at all, except to enjoy the good times while living off unemployment insurance benefits? Or of cases of fraud where workers who have a job keep receiving UI benefits?
The proposed reform, Mr. Speaker, must aim at remedy this kind of abuse, but must also give a new direction to Canadians by encouraging them to actively search for new jobs. The reform must give Canadians new hope and means to find work. This reform will guide us, Mr. Speaker! As we enter the era of free trade, we will increase our efforts by directing additionnal funds toward the training of our workers.

subsubtopic: IMPACT OF PROPOSED CHANGES ON CONSTITUENTS OF KOOTENAY EAST
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to comment on the impact of the Government's recent announcement of changes to the unemployment insurance system on the people of my riding. Many of my constituents are employed in seasonal occupations such as construction, tourism, forestry and the fruit industry. These people play a vital role in the local economy of the East Kootenays. During the off-season, which differs depending on the industry, many seasonal workers depend on unemployment insurance benefits to make ends meet.
Under the past system I had over 80 inquiries relating to UIC. The majority of them come from women employed in seasonal jobs. It is one of the single biggest issues I have dealt with since my election.
While I have no problems with increased funding for retraining, I object to additional funding to be paid for by the unemployed of my riding and the country as a whole. It is clear that the needs of my constituents and the citizens across Canada will be ignored.
My final observation is that if the Government wants to cut the deficit on the backs of the unemployed, it should be up front about it instead of portraying the new system as a measure to help unemployed Canadians.

Mr. Speaker, I want to commend the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mrs. McDougall) for the announced changes in Canada's Unemployment Insurance Program. In particular, I want to commend the Government for its continuing commitment to worker training programs and job-creation. The future of our country does rest on a skilled and disciplined workforce, and the Minister's priorities are directed to the appropriate areas to achieve this. The fragility of Atlantic Canada's economy was not overlooked.
The announced changes are moving us in the right direction as we prepare to enter the 21st Century.

subsubtopic: DONATIONS TO CANADIAN ALLIANCE FOR TRADE AND JOB OPPORTUNITIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, during the federal election the so-called nonpartisan Canadian Alliance for Trade and Job Opportunities, the primary pro-free trade lobby, spent $5.2 million on behalf of the Conservative Government and the free trade proposal.
I and Mr. Hurtig of the Canadian Council had the audacity to challenge the Council suggesting this was one way for large U.S.-owned multinationals to interfere in the Canadian election process. We were promised there would be full disclosure of where their donations came from. Mr. D'Aquino, the hired gun for the Alliance, had this to say in a letter to every Canadian newspaper. He ". . .looked forward to reading a public retraction. . .when the list of donors is made public next year".

April 12, 1989
Oral Questions
We learned yesterday that some big Canadian corporations, Noranda, Shell and others, donated $250,000. The Royal Bank was a little measly. It only put $200,000 into the pot. All the foreign-owned and controlled corporations refused to disclose what kind of contributions they made to that Alliance.
This represents a serious threat to Canadian democracy. It is a silent, invisible, alternative form of government. I suggest it is time we reform the Elections Act.

subsubtopic: FEDERAL FUNDING FOR BARRIE AND DISTRICT INDUSTRIAL TRAINING COUNCIL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise before you today with great pleasure and excitement to inform my fellow Members of an historic initiative which occurred in my riding of Simcoe Centre this past Friday.
On behalf of the Hon. Barbara McDougall, Minister of Employment and Immigration, I had the honour of announcing federal funding to the Barrie and District Industrial Training Council that will be used to help launch an experimental project in participating high schools throughout the Simcoe County School District.
Skills Canada is intended to improve the image of manufacturing careers and provide an incentive for students to pursue technical careers boosting the sagging enrollment in many technical colleges and schools and providing technical workers for industrial growth.
This program is unique in Canada. Our Government has shown innovative leadership by providing these start-up funds.
The private sector's initiative is the best catalyst for economic growth, and Skills Canada is a positive and cost-effective method by which the private sector can work in concert with the Government towards educating more skilled workers among the youth of Canada.

speakeroldname: Hon. Bill McKnight (Minister of National Defence):
subtopic: DEPLOYMENT OF PEACEKEEPING FORCES TO NAMIBIA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on this occasion to deposit in the Chamber an Order in Council approving the deployment of Canadian forces in support of the United Nations peacekeeping operation in Namibia.
I would like to take this opportunity to once again underline the importance that this Government attaches to international peacekeeping and peaceful resolution of disputes. Much has been made in recent months about the radical improvement in international relations. This is best reflected in the increased rhythm of peacekeeping activity in various parts of the world.
My colleague and predecessor, the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Beatty), stood in this House only last September and again in December to comment on Canada's peacekeeping efforts around the world and to comment again on the dedication and commitment of our Canadian Forces members to the cause of peace in foreign countries near and far.
Canada has participated in virtually every peacekeeping operation undertaken by the United Nations since the end of the Second World War. Canadian peacekeepers currently serve in such far-off places as Cyprus, Syria, the Sinai, Iran and Iraq, Afghanistan and now Namibia.
Later this afternoon, the largest contingent of troops will be on their way to Namibia. I know these men and women and their families are acutely aware of the magnitude of the tasks facing them and their individual responsibilities for the success of this mission. They know of the important role they play in preserving peace in that region and ensuring the independence of the world's newest nation. They also know of the proud tradition of Canadian peacekeepers who have gone before them and of the respect and the appreciation of the world for their efforts.
I would also like to point out to my colleagues that we have this week responded to an additional call from the United Nations above and beyond our troop commitments and will be providing additional air support for the speedy deployment of the UN force.
Peace is a precious thing. It needs to be nurtured. It needs to be cultivated with patience and with diligence. It is hard sometimes and at times it is dangerous work. It cannot be taken for granted. Canada is committed to this task, and when the United Nations has asked for our assistance in the past, we have not hesitated to respond. We will not hesitate to respond in the future.
I know that all Hon. Members wish to join in offering our best wishes and support to the Canadian peacekeepers. I cannot think of a more appropriate role for our forces and for our nation.

Mr. Speaker, on behalf of the New Democratic Party, I welcome the Minister's announcement. We share with the Government and Canadians the considerable pride we have in the role our Canadian Forces have played in peace-keeping operations around the world. That they are serving with distinction whether in Cyprus, Syria, the Sinai, Iran, Iraq or Afghanistan signifies the commitment of Canadians to the peaceful resolution of disputes. It is the reason why our Forces are recipients of the Nobel Peace Prize.
In the case of Namibia, as recent events attest, Canadian troops are entering a sensitive and dangerous situation. They are there to oversee the implementation of Namibian independence resulting from negotiations which did not involve the Namibian Contact group, of which Canada is a member, nor the UN Council for Namibia, but rather Angola, Cuba and South Africa. SWAPO and the myriad South African occupying forces have been engaged in bloody conflict. This is partially a result of confusion surrounding the peace process, perhaps exploited by both sides. It is equally the result of the failure of the Security Council, of which Canada is a member, to ensure speedy deployment of UNTAG forces in sufficient numbers.
Canada is highly respected in southern Africa. Its participation in UNTAG will be welcomed. However, the safety and effectiveness of our Forces as well as Canada's prestige will depend upon Canada's role in restoring trust and confidence in the role of the UN itself. That will require that the strength of UNTAG forces be set at the agreed upon level of 7,500 persons. It will depend upon ensuring that the elections are not controlled by South Africa but by the United Nations, and that there be a stop to South African manipulation and intimidation. The purpose of this Bill is to make the office of the Auditor General a more current and effective institution by allowing it to report comprehensive audits as they are completed, rather than once a year as at present.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it gives me great pleasure to rise for my first time in this House to respond to the Speech from the Throne.
First, I would like to say how proud I am to have been elected to the House of Commons and to represent the people of Canada's most populated riding, the riding of York North. Getting here, I must say, was a bit difficult. As a matter of fact, I am perhaps the only Member in the House who had to win the same election twice before he could take his seat. I think my experience has given me a greater appreciation for the meaning of the often heard expression "better late than never".
No greater honour can be bestowed upon a Canadian than to have been elected by one's fellow citizens to the Parliament of Canada. This was possible only because of the overwhelming support I received from the hard working, compassionate and caring people who reside in the riding of York North. I am extremely grateful to them for their vote of confidence and their expression of faith in my candidacy.
I pledge to my constituents that I will carry out the duties and responsibilities associated with being a Member of Parliament to the best of my abilities. I will devote my full energies with integrity, honesty and compassion as we attempt to build a strong and just Canadian society.
At this point, I must take some time to thank all those people who devoted time and energy and their commitment to my campaign, and more important to the cause and division that it represented. I am a Member of Parliament today because of those people.

April 12, 1989
The Address-Mr. Bevdacqua
Also kindly permit me to thank those people who have been very close to me throughout my life, my wife, Ellena, my son Jean-Paul, my parents, my sister, my brothers and my in-laws. Without their help, I would not have been able to sit in this Elouse.
If would like to say a few words about the riding of York North. I guess it can be best described as a dynamic socially and economically diverse area just north of Metropolitan Toronto. It is Canada's most populated riding consisting of four large townships, Aurora, Richmond Hill, Vaughn and King with an estimated population of approximately 180,000. It is a very interesting community of urban and rural regions creating a unique environment.
As I mentioned earlier my journey to Ottawa was not an easy one, but I must say that I was very pleased to hear in the Speech from the Throne that the Government will appoint a commission of inquiry to make recommendations for needed changes and reforms to the electoral laws. I endorse their initiative. However, I must make veiy clear that that endorsement is conditional on the reform and that changes to the legislation be effective before the next general election. I hope that the commission does not become merely another way to further delay the progress in this very important and fundamental area of legislation.
Last April 3 when I finally got to the House of Commons, I realized that many years ago when I chose the Liberal Party of Canada as my political home, I made the right choice because it was the Liberal Party of Canada that allowed the son of an immigrant worker to seek public office, the Party that chose inclusion over exclusion. I have always believed that participation in political life in our nation is a passion and a vocation, and that the true politician is one who exercises that passion by fighting for causes that reflect the progressive vision of Canada of moving this country ahead without leaving anyone behind. I chose the Liberal Party as my political home because my faith in this philosophy, our belief in liberalism, gives us the strength to confront the powerful, to challenge the status quo, to question and seek the truth. Our faith in our Party has given us the strength to fight against anything and anyone that attempts to prevent the fulfilment of our dreams as citizens of this country.
Our Party has traditionally been the Party of reconciliation reaching out to unfairly treated minorities, to the dissatisfied regions, to disadvantaged groups of all kind and responding to their needs without alienating other segments of Canadian society.
In this Parliament today we meet at a crossroads, not at a point of arrival, but a point of departure. Where do we go from here? We must act on an agenda that challenges this generation as previous problems challenged our forefathers.
I see that agenda in the face of the single mother, who, with her children, has to stand in front of the local food bank for their daily meal. I see it in the apprehension of the 45 year-old factory worker who understands the personal threat imposed by this Government's insensitive free trade deal. I see it in the inequity of this Government's budget which has unfairly burdened our middle class while rewarding the chosen few. I see it in a failure to crack down on our drug problem which is ruining many young lives. I see it in the hurt the people feel when they are denied rightful opportunities because of discrimination based on sex, race, religion or ethnic origin and the frustration that they feel knowing that their children will be unfairly carrying the baggage of this ugly reality.
I see it in the human sufferings in South Africa, in Ethiopia, in the Middle East which cry out for a politics of caring and humanity. I see it in a country as rich as ours where there are still people without shelter, food or proper medical care.

subsubtopic: RESUMPTION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: RESUMPTION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
I see it in the sad eyes of the child sitting on the steps alone waiting for her parents to come home because our country fails to see the light when it comes to a national day care program.
While the Speech from the Throne used forceful language when talking about spending cuts, it was deliberately vague in reference to programs that might involve new money. If we are to plan for the future of Canada, we better start with the growing need for quality child care. The Government should recognize this and begin to plan for the future.
My concerns are obvious. We must decide what type of society we want to live in. Do we want a market-driven, profit comes first, people-last society or a compassionate, caring society that rewards people's efforts yet has the ability to help the weak and the disadvantaged.
April 12, 1989	COMMONS
Therefore, when I went to the Senate to hear the Speech from the Throne, I noticed that the over-all focus of this Government was on deficit reduction, and that reducing the deficit is of vital necessity if Canada's economic well- being is to be secured.
I would like, first of all, to be on the record as an individual who believes in the importance of being fiscally responsible. However, I sense that deficit reduction has become such a tunnel-vision view that I fear it will overwhelm all other issues mentioned or not mentioned in the Speech from the Throne. I am also wondering why this Government, that is going to raise taxes and cut spending, never told the Canadian people during the election campaign.
Over the past four years Canadians have been subjected to the sharpest tax hikes in Canada's history. These increases were introduced in spite of promises to the contrary. The speech was deliberately vague on what tax changes might be expected, but very clear that the taxes will occur. I wonder why this Government cannot tell Canadians exactly what it intends to do instead of keeping Canadians in the dark.

subsubtopic: RESUMPTION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: RESUMPTION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
I conclude my remarks by saying that the Throne Speech needs to be seriously examined by all Canadians. There is no reference to federal programs for housing or disposable federal land holdings for affordable housing or how the courts will deal with the Youth Offenders Act. No timetable for legislation was given.
Having the honour of being appointed associate critic for youth, I would be remiss in not mentioning the greatest resource Canada has as being in fact our youth.
I firmly believe that all government policy should take into consideration the impact that it has on youth and the environment. We must continue to establish programs which encourage young people to acquire skills necessary to meet the future demands of our economy.
Drug use in Canada, especially among our youth, continues to rise. I strongly support drug prevention programs and increased law enforcement to bring this problem under control.
Finally, I want to congratulate all Members in the House on their election. Let them always be mindful of the responsibilities we have toward Canadians and to never forget that what we do and, more important, what we do not do, seriously affects the future of this country.

The Address-Mr. Bevilacqua
Canada is many people, many regions, many cultures and many ideas, with one thing in common: we all strive to attain economic and social justice. It is our responsibility to achieve it.

The fourth fundamental objective listed by the Government in the Speech from the Throne is to foster a confident sense of Canada's culture and national uniqueness in which Canadians may have a greater sense of their common values and common citizenship.
As my colleague will know, this country was largely built against forces dragging us toward the United States. We have traditionally used such tools as the construction and maintenance of a national railway in order to keep the various parts of our country together.
I represent Glengarry, in which there is the town of Alexandria. It was founded by Father Alexander Macdo-nell in the early 1800s. Have you ever heard the story Of how Brian came to shame I'll tell you so you'll understand He is trying to scrap our trains

speechtext:
I want to thank the Hon. Member for Glengarry-Prescott-Russell (Mr. Boudria) for his question. It seems to me that now more than ever it is important to maintain a sense of national identity as Canadians.
Historically, I believe the railway has been something which has maintained that very essential nationhood that is Canada. It is also important that when we talk about the railway we also talk about the people in the multicultural diversity of Canada who use those railways to see what Canada is all about.
With respect to the issue of multiculturalism, I think the time has come for us to begin to review our policy and look at Canadians as equal partners in building this great land. During the election I began to look at new ways to deal with the social reality of Canada in cultural terms. I began to see that indeed we must review the policy of multiculturalism, to make it all-embracing rather than perhaps risk it becoming a policy of ghettoi-zation. By that, I mean when we talk about the policy of multiculturalism we should be talking about English and French Canadians in the same way as we talk about Italian, Portuguese and Greek Canadians.
I think it is time to initiate a policy that perhaps looks at the establishment of a super ministry of culture that will bring in everyone throughout the country.
We have talked about the railway and the people. I think they are both important elements in Canada.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in my first address to the House I want to begin by congratulating you upon your appointment and the Speaker for his election to office. I was privileged to have been able to work for the Speaker during his term as Minister of Fisheries and Oceans. He governed for the whole country with distinction and my respect for him has only grown in the short time I have been in this Chamber. Once again, I offer my congratulations and best wishes.
I would also like to congratulate the mover of the Address to the Speech from the Throne, the Member for Calgary Southeast (Mr. Richardson), and the seconder, the Member for Bourassa (Mrs. Gibeau), for their significant and thoughtful remarks. While the Member for Calgary Southeast and I often disagree in our views on hockey-he actually thinks the Flames might beat the Oilers-we stand together in our support for the recent Speech from the Throne.
I would also like to take this opportunity to thank my constituents of Edmonton-Strathcona for their support during the past election. I look forward to serving this recently redistributed constituency which encompasses the south centre of the City of Edmonton. It includes the historic old Strathcona area, the home of the Frinse Theatre Festival, the famous Strathcona Hotel and the Princess Theatre.
Historically, the City of Strathcona amalgamated with the City of Edmonton in 1912. At one time the riding of Strathcona went as far east as Lloydminster, and so far south that it almost went to Calgary.
Edmonton-Strathcona shares with the rest of the city the beauty of the wide and deep North Saskatchewan River whose valley is reserved for parkland, playgrounds, picnic areas and golf courses.
My riding is home to the University of Alberta, the second largest university in this country, a world-class institution with world-class scholars and facilities. The university is keenly interested in our Government's science and technology initiatives and is looking forward to becoming partners with the federal Government in a number of endeavours. I am here to make that happen.
Also a part of Edmonton-Strathcona is the Walter C. MacKenzie Health Sciences Centre, a state of the art hospital with enormous teaching and research facilities. It, too, is excited about many of our Government's initiatives.
April 12, 1989

The City of Strathcona was named after Donald Smith, Lord Strathcona and Mount Royal, who drove the last spike of the CPR home. Lord Strathcona also served our country with distinction as a Conservative Member of this House. One might say that Conservative roots in Edmonton-Strathcona run deep. As a railway magnate, he contributed to the building of the Canadian Pacific Railway, the impossible dream which joined Canada from sea to sea and made this country truly united.
It was the railway which facilitated settlement to the west and it is the railway which continues to play a vital role in the western economy and way of life. It is for this reason that my constituents and indeed all westerners support the survival of the VIA Rail service in our communities.
As a new Member, it is an honour for me to participate in the discussion on the speech given by the Governor General last week in the Senate Chamber. The people of Edmonton-Strathcona and all Canadians know this to be a Government of action and initiative and are looking for policies which will enable Canada to better compete in world markets. This is where the future prosperity of our country lies. This is why Canadians voted last November in support of the Free Trade Agreement with the United States. Canadians realized that liberalized trade was necessary to guarantee a healthier economy.
A first step toward this goal is the adoption of a strong commitment to increasing research and development. Canada must pursue an aggressive stance in the area of science and technology. Much has already been done. On March 12, 1987, Canada's first ever national science and technology policy initiative was signed by federal, provincial and territorial Governments. This project is to be commended in that it acknowledges at all levels of Government the importance of technological advancement to Canada.
As well, the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) announced the creation of a national advisory board for science and technology. Its purpose is to offer the Government honest suggestions for the improvement of the status of science and technology in Canada. The Prime Minister himself is the chairman.
In addition, in January of 1988 the Government announced a Centres of Excellence program to encourage research and development in universities. This move signals a recognition of the importance of ongoing research at post-secondary institutions. The University of Alberta is looking forward to participating in this program.
The Address-Mr. Thorkelson
As part of the commitment of the Edmonton government caucus to this purpose, a task force on science and technology and economic development in Edmonton is currently being put together. It will consider ways of bringing increased federal participation in research and development to the City of Edmonton. I must commend my caucus colleagues for putting together this task force.
Advances in science and technology are important, but these exciting initiatives cannot take place if measures to control Canada's debt are not vigorously pursued. During the past week of debate on the Throne Speech, much has been said about the deficit and the importance of reducing it. On April 27, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) will announce this Government's Budget. A plan which will address the urgency Canadians feel toward the debt problem, a plan which emphasizes restraint and which will include measures to reduce the deficit and bring Canadians out from under the burden of the previous fiscal mismanagement, will be introduced.
It is mind-boggling, to say the least, when one considers that 31 cents of every dollar of government revenue go toward annual interest payments. Money is being borrowed solely to pay interest on the debt of the past. How can any Government pursue effective programs for the well-being of its citizens with such an oppressive weight upon it? It is my conviction and the conviction of this Government that this burden must be lifted. It will be lifted.
The Government further demonstrates its commitment to ensuring a better Canada for its young people through its acknowledgement of the necessity of addressing our environmental problems. We are spoiled here in Canada in that we enjoy a nation diverse in the character of its regions: the warm beauty of the western coast, the stark challenge of the Rockies, the rolling prairies, the sprawling urban centres in Ontario and Quebec and the historic surroundings of Atlantic Canada. These are precious features of our country, a proud legacy which we must protect for future generations.
This Government has illustrated its resolution to safeguarding Canada's environment and has committed itself to policies which reflect the concept of sustainable development, an exciting proposal in which economic policies are not removed from their environmental impact. This Government's endorsement of sustainable development demonstrates a commitment to pursue policies which do not treat economics and the environment as independent of each other.

April 12, 1989
The Address-Mr. Thorkelson
The creation of the National Round Table on the Environment and the Economy as well as initiatives mentioned in the Throne Speech, such as the intention to limit the impact of toxic chemicals through regulations in the Canadian Environmental Protection Act, the creation of a centre for the international promotion of sustainable development to be located in Winnipeg, the promotion of environmentally friendly products and others are policies which the citizens of Edmonton- Strathcona and indeed all of Canada encourage and support. They are important for today and important for tomorrow as well.
Canada's future, for that is what we have been discussing this past week, will be shaped through our ability to adjust and compete in the technologies of tomorrow. It will be shaped through our ability to reduce and manage our deficit. It will be shaped too by our ability to accept responsibility for the damage being done to the environment and to reverse the frightening trends of today.
Canada's future will be shaped as well by our ability to face the challenges of constitutional change. The Meech Lake Accord has provided Canadians with the opportunity to strengthen our Constitution and to reinforce national unity. For the people of Edmonton-Strathcona, our Government's commitment to this purpose brings Senate reform that much closer to its realization.
Our Government has supported western Canada and has done much to alleviate western feelings of alienation. It was our Government that ended the National Energy Program, a Liberal program which crippled the western economy. It was our Government which eliminated the PGRT, a tax that devastated the oil sector in the West. It was our Government which put an end to discriminatory freight rates which favoured central Canada. Our Government has provided the avenue for the meaningful Senate reform the West has been seeking.
Last December, I rose in this House to express my wholehearted support for the Triple-E concept of reform of the Senate. I reaffirm today my commitment to that proposal and encourage those who are working, as I am, for a Senate which is elected, equal and effective. Only through election can the Senate have the mandate
to act in the manner originally defined for it. Only through equal representation can the Senate ensure that the concerns of each province are heard. Only through redefining the powers of the Senate can it be made effective in its intended role.
The Speech from the Throne has made clear the commitment this Government has to improving Canada's ability to hold its own in a world grown more competitive in its nature. There are many challenges ahead that this Government is dedicated to meeting, challenges which this Government must address to ensure a prosperous future for all of Canada.

Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member, who is a newcomer to the House like myself and many other Members, took a very broad view and referred to all the regions in this country, something I appreciated very much. He spoke to environmental issues among other things. I am referring to the Hon. Member for Edmonton-Strathcona (Mr. Thorkelson), one of the youngest Members in this House.
I would like to ask him the following question. He made a reference to the Meech Lake Accord. Considering the political climate in this country when the Liberals were in power, when we had almost total confrontation between the federal Government and the provinces, how does he see a re-elected Conservative Government as being instrumental in making Canada the united country it was before Liberal attempts to achieve the opposite?

subsubtopic: RESUMPTION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
I want to thank the Hon. Member for his question. I agree that before the Meech Lake Accord was arrived at, there was much dissension and conflict within our federal system. The people in western Canada for the most part support the Meech Lake Accord because it helps Canadians shape their own destiny. It helps communities achieve their own aspirations and goals.
The Meech Lake Accord puts Senate reform at the top of the constitutional agenda, which is very important to western Canada. Premiers, by submitting lists of names to the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney), have an input into an important institution. In Alberta, Premier Getty has indicated he will hold an election to help him put together a list for the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney). I support this. The people of Alberta support this. I
April 12, 1989

believe we will have our first election for a senator next fall during the civic elections. I encourage the Premier of Alberta to go forward with a plan to elect a nominee and submit a list with that nominee, the second runner-up and the third runner-up, to the Prime Minister.

speechtext:
I want to congratulate the new Member on his speech. We have much in common. We are both interested in research and development. I appreciate it when the Hon. Member says we should be working together in order to improve in this area. The idea of a task force in Edmonton is a great one, and I hope the Government will get the signal from what is happening in Edmonton and start task forces all across the nation. I believe many of the solutions are in the hands of the communities. The communities know what needs to be done. They need tools provided by the Government. They need incentives and assistance programs.
I was involved with the research and development industry for a number of years. We have companies we can be proud of, Northern Telecom and others. This industry is penetrating the Japanese market like never before. It is prospering in the North American and European markets. Assistance in that field would be appreciated. The Hon. Member through his caucus and committee work should push the Government to invest more in research and development.
I am in total agreement with the Hon. Member that we have to save VIA Rail. We must work collectively to save VIA Rail. It is a reflection of what Canada is all about. It is the link that connects the east and west. It is a symbol of Canadian unity. It is a part of Canadian heritage.
My question to the Hon. Member is, how will you pressure the Government to save VIA Rail?

subsubtopic: RESUMPTION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
I have indicated my support for VIA Rail. It was the railway that built the west. It continues to play a very important role in western Canada, moving goods in and out of western Canada.
The Edmonton-Jasper-Vancouver run is very important. Many Japanese tourists come into Edmonton. They take the train overnight through the Rockies. VIA Rail is very important to tourism.
The Address-Mr. Thorkelson
I have discussed my support for VIA Rail with my caucus colleagues and discussions are ongoing. However, we must wait and analyse the global impact of other programs. We must be efficient.
With respect to science and technology, I thank you for your comments. I will direct them to our caucus. Our caucus has been supportive and pro-active in putting together a task force. We hope we can come to a consensus of where we should specialize in science and technology in Edmonton. In Alberta we have a resource base. We want to add knowledge and value to that. We need to examine the whole question. When we do that, I will report the findings of this task force to the House.

speechtext:
The Hon. Member mentioned the matter of deficit reduction. One of the banner programs the Government is contemplating is the imposition of a new national super sales tax estimated to generate between $8 billion and $10 billion in new revenue each year. That is approximately $1,000 a year for the average Canadian family.
The National Council on Welfare has informed us that for a family earning $100,000 a year, the sales taxes currently in place in Canada will gobble up approximately 4 per cent of that family's annual income. If they are earning $40,000 a year, sales taxes will take better than 6 per cent of their income. If they are struggling and trying to manage on $10,000 a year, that family will pay approximately 11.5 per cent of its income in sales taxes.
The Conservative Government of the Province of Alberta is implacably opposed to the imposition of this new national sales tax, as has been stated by Premier Getty, Alberta's Treasurer, Mr. Johnston, and by the New Democratic Party in Alberta. I will not pretend to speak for the Liberal Party in Alberta. They seem to have trouble determining that themselves.
Given all of this, given the nearly unanimous opposition to the creation of an at-the-till sales tax in Alberta for the first time, will the Hon. Member oppose the tax in this House?

subsubtopic: RESUMPTION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
I would like to thank the Hon. Member for his five-minute question on the sales tax issue. The Hon. Member should know that when the sales tax, business transfer tax or value added tax is finally implemented, the 3 per cent surcharge on our taxes will come off. There will be tax credits for low-income Canadians.

April 12, 1989
The Address-Miss D. Grey
One of the issues in this proposed national sales tax program is that we have a patchwork across the nation of different goods; some are taxed and some are not. It will be a lower rate, more broadly applied. In Alberta there is an awful lot of capital investment in the oil industry, in manufacturing and in other industries, that are taxed at a high rate. The rate will be lower. There will greater economic growth.
No, I am not opposed to the imposition of a business transfer tax, or a value added tax, or a new equitable and fairer sales tax.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as a new Member speaking for the first time in the House of Commons, I wish to congratulate and thank those who make this institution what it is.
I wish to congratulate the Speaker on his re-election as Speaker of the House, and sincerely thank him and the House staff for all the help and assistance they provide to new Members.
I wish to congratulate the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulro-ney) and each Member of the Government on their re-election and, as a western Canadian, thank them for their willingness to pursue the free trade initiative.
I also wish to congratulate the leaders and Members of the Official Opposition and the New Democratic Party on their re-election.
In particular, I want to thank the Hon. Member for Gloucester (Mr. Young), and the Hon. Member for Edmonton East (Mr. Harvey), for introducing me to the House on Monday, April 3.
I would also like to extend my condolences to the family and friends of Beaver River's original Member-elect, Mr. John Dahmer, whose untimely death necessitated the by-election in our riding.
I am especially pleased to note that the word "reform" is creeping into the Government's vocabulary, and appears at least four times in the Speech from the Throne in reference to tax reform, reform of Canada's legal system, parliamentary reform, and reform of the electoral process.
The word "reform" means constructive change and represents a long and honourable tradition in Canadian politics from coast to coast.
It was the reform parties and reformers of Upper and Lower Canada and Atlantic Canada who secured representative and responsible Government for the Canadian colonies, and thus laid the foundation for Confederation.
In the West there have been five major reform movements since 1870: Riel and the Metis, Haultain and the Independents, the Progressive Party, and the Depression Parties of Social Credit and the CCF. Each of these played a distinctive role in advancing western economic, social, and constitutional interests within Confederation.
As the first elected Member of the new Reform Party of Canada, I hope to build upon this great tradition and bring a fresh and positive perspective to the deliberations of the House and the analysis of the Government's Speech from the Throne.
Most importantly, I wish to take this opportunity to congratulate and thank the people of Beaver River for their willingness to be political pioneers.
Beaver River is a new federal riding in Alberta stretching from just east of Edmonton all the way to the Saskatchewan border. It encompasses an area of approximately 28,000 square kilometres inhabited by approximately 72,000 people.
Its three most basic industries are agriculture, energy and forestry. Our towns and businesses provide goods and services to these industries and the people employed by them. We also service a growing tourist trade attracted by our numerous and beautiful northern lakes.
Communities of Beaver River include Namao and Cold Lake, each the site of a major armed services base. Beaver River includes farming communities of Gibbons, Smoky Lake, Warspite, Thorhild and Waskatenau, many of them established and settled by pioneers of Ukrainian origin.
Beaver River includes the town and oil fields of Redwater, the site of a major oil strike in Alberta after Leduc. It includes the towns of Grand Centre, Bonny-ville, and Elk Point in the heart of Alberta's heavy oil country.
Beaver River is the home of seven major Indian reserves and four Metis colonies. It includes the towns of Lac la Biche, soon to be the site of a new pulp mill, and St. Paul, one of the oldest francophone communities in Alberta.
April 12, 1989

I am pleased to report that grassroots democracy is alive and well in Beaver River. Our people, in the recent by-election, seriously considered and expressed themselves on several of the major items contained in the Speech from the Throne, items which ought to have become major issues in the general election, but unfortunately did not because of the preoccupation with free trade.
Rightly or wrongly, many of our people believe that the legislative programs of the federal Government are too centralized in their orientation, focused on managing Toronto's economic boom and meeting Quebec's constitutional demands, to the neglect of the needs and interests of the more thinly populated resource producing areas of the country.
Rightly or wrongly, many of our people believe that the processes whereby the federal Government makes policy and decisions are executive processes dominated by that arm of the Government and beyond the reach or involvement of the common people.
For example, our people feel utterly powerless to influence the high interest rate policy of the Bank of Canada, or the imposition of a national sales tax, despite the fact that our businesses, home-owners, and taxpayers simply cannot afford to pay more interest and more taxes.
Our people are not unsympathetic to constitutional amendments to make Quebec more at home in Confederation, but they want concurrent constitutional amendments, namely, meaningful Senate reform to make the West feel more at home in Confederation.
In the past generation, Mr. Speaker, it is the West which has experienced the National Energy Program and the CF-18 decision, not Quebec. It is the West's grievances which the Government should be addressing with at least as much fervour as it brings to Quebec's demands.
In its present form, the Meech Lake Accord thus fails completely to win the support of the people of the West, and the executive dominated process under which the Meech Lake Accord was developed is even more unattractive to our people than its contents.
To us, Meech Lake is not an example of democratic constitution building, but executive federalism run amok. Professor Schwartz of the University of Manitoba says Canada is moving towards government "of the govern-
The Address-Miss D. Grey
ment, by the government, and for the government". The Beaver River, I must report, Mr. Speaker, is not a tributary of Meech Lake. Its waters come from different sources and How in a different direction.
I will be distributing summaries of the Government's Throne Speech and Budget Speech throughout Beaver River. I will be holding meetings in all our major communities to discuss these important documents. I shall then undertake to report back to the House, not necessarily what I think, not simply what my Party thinks, but what the people of Beaver River think about the Government's legislative program and budgetary measures.
The people of Beaver River are not as partisan as those of us here. They will not denounce the Government's legislative program as the embodiment of all evil and perversity, as some Hon. Members have done. Nor will they eulogize the Government's program as the embodiment of all virtue and wisdom, as other Hon. Members have done.
They will be more objective. They will ask and expect answers to simple, blunt, common-sense questions concerning each of the Government's legislative and budgetary proposals.
They will ask: Is it necessary? Is it fair? Who gets help and who gets hurt? Is it practical? What does it cost? Can we afford it?
I know my fellow citizens of Beaver River well enough that I can anticipate at least some of their reactions to the contents of the Speech from the Throne. For example, they will welcome the Government's commitment to environmental conservation, though they will wonder how it will work in practice.
They will welcome the Government's commitment to a strong economy and deficit reduction, but they will be looking for signs of real cost-cutting at the top, and in the thick layer of middle management that characterizes so many Government programs, before they will be willing to make sacrifices at their level.
They will frown as they read the words that the new federal sales tax is to be "fair and equitable", and they will not believe such words. Our people, you see, Mr. Speaker, were told that the National Energy Program, followed by two years of the Petroleum Gas Revenue Tax, were to be fair and equitable, programs and taxes which crippled the economy of Beaver River.

April 12, 1989
The Address-Miss D. Grey
They will laugh, especially the Indian people, when they read that the Government believes "extending its programs to assist native economic development" will enable native people to "participate fully in Canada's economic development projects". The current programs, they say, simply do not work.
Lastly, the people of Beaver River will ask about the gaps in the Speech from the Throne. For example, they will wonder why there is no clear directive from the Government to the Bank of Canada concerning interest rates which are working immense hardship among small businesses and home-owners in the regions of the country where the economy is certainly not over-heated, and has not been for a long time.
They will also ask why the Government does not feel, in response to the demands of western Canadians, the same sense of urgency to pursue meaningful Senate reform as it feels in pursuing Meech Lake in response to the demands of Quebec. They will ask why the Government insists on subordinating Senate reform to the Meech Lake Accord.
I would ask the Government and the Members of this House to regard the concerns of the people of Beaver River as they would those of their own constituencies. The people of Beaver River are uneasy patriots, and look forward to the day when they become truly fair and equitable partners in confederation.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to start off by congratulating our hon. colleague, the Member for Beaver River (Miss Grey), both in her speech and, of course, on her election. The Hon. Member is the most recent Member to be elected to the House of Commons. I think I speak on behalf of all Members when I offer the Hon. Member our congratulations.
The Hon. Member speaks of the executive type of federalism that we have, which I believe was the expression used in her speech. She was obviously speaking of the ever-increasing power of the Cabinet over the other institutions of our country, namely, Parliament. I wonder if the Member has yet had an opportunity to acquaint herself with the fact that, contrary to tradition, the Government usually requests in the Throne Speech that Parliament grant Supply. In other words, from time to
time Parliament gives the Government money in order to operate. This Throne Speech does not include those key words, which are not only very traditional and historic, but are part of the conventions of how we operate as a Parliament.
Second, I want to bring the following proposition to the Member. The Government had an obligation to bring in Estimates, and to obtain Supply from Parliament last winter. In other words, to obtain funds in order to operate. Instead of doing that, the Government chose to prorogue Parliament in order not to have to go through the series of Supply days, or opposition days, as we commonly refer to them here. Instead, they prorogued Parliament and did not return until now. They went to see the Governor General in order to get an executive warrant to obtain funds in order to continue the operations of Government, rather than to ask this Parliament, the way we are supposed to do it under our conventions.

subsubtopic: RESUMPTION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: That is what Premier Getty did in Alberta, too.

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Liberal Party
subsubtopic: RESUMPTION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
The Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Turner) expresses the fact that that is what the Leader of the Government in Alberta had done as well.
I want to ask our new colleague if she does not agree with me that it is time we gave back to Parliament not only new powers, as some people are talking about, but at least restore the powers to Parliament that it has traditionally had in our country. I thought these powers still existed until I came to the sad realization only a few short days ago in this House that this Government, during the last recess, had made many of the powers we formerly had disappear by that one request for Supply to the Governor General, instead of seeking that consent from Parliament.

I think what we are talking about is what should the federal Government be doing in terms of executive federalism. I do not want to comment on the whole idea of Supply. Obviously, I am not going to be arrogant enough to assume that I know everything that goes on in the House. What I will say is I think the triangle of true democracy has been inverted, whereby when we are looking in the social studies textbooks at elected representatives going to Ottawa with their constituents' concerns, unfortunately that triangle has become inverted. We believe very strongly in direct representation by the people. What we have seen is that
April 12, 1989

triangle upside down, with Government sending their representatives back to their home constituencies with Ottawa's words for them. That triangle is inverted.

Thank you, Mr. Speaker. I would just like to offer my congratulations to the new Member for Beaver River. The Member speaks about the deficit and the problem of controlling spending. The Member also suggested that one of the areas of concern is middle management. My question to the Member is this: What percentage of government spending goes into what you call middle management? What specific Departments would you recommend or suggest for cutting spending in these areas?
The Address-Mr. Axworthy

subsubtopic: RESUMPTION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY

Your point is well taken. I do not have figures in terms of exactly how many dollars are allocated to that. What we are concerned about is a symbolic gesture from the top which would say that we in the higher ranking echelons are willing to tighten our belts and make some personal sacrifices, thereby sending a signal to the man on the street. I have to speak personally and say that at 36 years of age I do not know that at age 42 I should be entitled to a fully indexed pension. If I choose not to get re-elected after that, or do not get re-elected, that is my prerogative. I could probably go back quite comfortably into the workforce.
Specifically, the Nielsen task force came up with 200 recommendations as to what could be done in terms of cutting out this thick layer at the top. There is a symbolic gesture. There is a real gesture, and there is a sense of taking advantage of the recommendations made by the Nielsen task force, many of which the Government has not acted on.

Does she think that contributing to that inverted triangle, as far as she is concerned, is an over heavy cabinet structure with 39 or 40 members, the largest cabinet structure in Canadian history? speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, let me begin by defending the Conservative Government from an unjust criticism made of it. Critics of the Government have claimed in the past that the Government has no philosophy and no ideas, that it is

April 12. 1989
The Address-Mr. Axworthy
driven solely by polls and that it has no vision of the country. This was finally disproved by the Speech from the Throne brought before the House on April 3. The Government has a well-defined philosophy, a neo-Conservative agenda that it is determined to force down the throats of every Canadian. No longer can it be said that the Government has a hidden agenda. The soft words of the Throne Speech barely cover the iron fist of the Conservative Government.
The Prime Minister's unctuous words cannot disguise the threats to ordinary Canadians promised by his Government. No longer will the economically disadvantaged be protected. No longer will a democratic government defend the sick, the unemployed, the poor, our first nations and our farmers. Instead, all will be subject to the iron discipline of the market-place where the strong survive and the losers are cast off.
No disadvantaged, no hard-pressed group of Canadians is safe from attack by this Government. We have seen that with the unemployed. We have seen it with Indian post-secondary students. Yet privileged groups, big business, the most well-off are safe. Billions in corporate deferred taxes are left alone. Some 60,000 Canadians who pay no tax are left alone. The rich who do not pay their fair share of taxes are not shouldering their fair burden of the deficit problem on which the Government is concentrating. Let us look at the Speech from the Throne and ask what the Government is saying and compare it with what the Government is doing.
For example, the Throne Speech indicates that the Government is convinced that the Canadian people will endorse its efforts to control federal spending in order to maintain economic stability and continued growth. Even if this is true, what does it say about the way the Government is going about it? In terms of the unemployment insurance changes, if yesterday is any indication the Canadian people disagree fundamentally. The rich and the powerful, such as the corporations, like the changes, but that is all. Ordinary folk, those who may need UIC after losing their jobs to free trade, global reorganization or whatever, do not like it. Neither do the three million people who used UIC last year, even though the majority of them used it through no fault of their own.
The Speech from the Throne carries on by stating that the Government believes fundamentally in those social benefits which support the family and the elderly while recognizing the need to direct more assistance toward those with low incomes. Yet through tax policy to date and the proposed national sales tax the Government continues to grab money from low-income Canadians. Through assistance cuts to the provinces the Government has reduced health services and social services available to them. On the one hand the Government talks about caring for Canadians while on the other hand it makes life more difficult for them.
The deficit is important. But there are many ways of dealing with it without attacking the less well-off. We should not forget that the Government has contributed over 50 per cent to the total deficit since 1984. Even though I am sure the Government is aware of other alternatives to cut the deficit, it continues to do so on the backs of less well-off Canadians and continues to ignore alternative suggestions which would be more fair and more appropriate.
I have three suggestions to make in this regard. We could deal with the interest rate. The Bank of Canada rate has risen from a low of 7.14 per cent in March of 1987 to over 12 per cent today. We all know that a 1 per cent reduction in interest rates reduces payments on the deficit by $1.5 billion. A slight easing of interest rates, maybe 1 per cent or 2 per cent, would help us avoid some of these problems. It would help us avoid a serious economic downturn which is a serious possibility in the regions of Canada. It would also assist in limiting the growth of the deficit. So there is room in interest rate policy to address the deficit.
Similarly, with regard to job creation and economic initiatives, austerity on the fiscal side has tended at least in the regions to choke economic growth. Anybody who wants to question that should spend some time in the regions. The Government seems to view as acceptable an unemployment rate of between 7.5 per cent and 8 per cent-over one million Canadians without work. Given that each 1 per cent drop in the jobless rate produces $2 billion in net federal revenues, action on this front is itself a deficit reduction strategy.
The Government has a responsibility to introduce effective policies and programs to generate high quality jobs, high paying jobs-not part-time jobs and not jobs in the service sector at minimum wage-particularly in
April 12, 1989

Canada's regions. Investments and upgrading municipal infrastructure, environmental protection, single-industry town diversification and research and development, for example, would not only create jobs but guarantee future income source.
What about the taxation system, a system which is becoming increasingly unfair? It is not one which is becoming more fair. In 1986, for example, the Auditor General estimated that the total annual value of personal and corporate tax breaks in the country was $28 billion. The Government could immediately move to limit or eliminate some corporate and personal tax breaks, contributing to the reduction of the deficit as well as to increasing public confidence in the tax system. We all know about corporate taxes, about profitable corporations paying no tax. We all know about rich Canadians who pay no tax. We all know that 1 per cent of the richest taxpayers in the country have had their taxes cut by the Government since 1984, while those less well-off have had to increase their tax burden. That is not a fair tax system. We could increase the fairness of the tax system and contribute to reduction of the deficit.
The Neilsen Task Force, as another Hon. Member pointed out, suggested that if we open Government procurement to more tendering we could save between a quarter and half a billion dollars a year.
Last, we might look at defence spending which has increased by over one-third in the four years since this Government took office in 1984, making defence one of the fastest growing areas of federal Government expenditure.
We do not need to attack the deficit by attacking those less well-off in society. We can find other ways. We can find other more fair ways.
From the beginning, the CCF and the NDP have articulated and put into practice the slogan, "people before profits". In doing so in my province, the Province of Saskatchewan, we have managed the government of the province in a way which has benefited people first and taken people first as an important agenda item. Government is about choices. Governments can put people first, or they might not. This Government has chosen not to. Saskatchewan, under the New Democratic Government, up until 1982 had lower taxes than it has now, higher social benefits and a balanced budget. Since the Progressive Conservative Government came to of-
The Address-Mr. Axworthy
fice, taxes have increased, social benefits have been reduced and a deficit has been created.
It is not necessary to take out the Government's deficit reduction program on the backs of less well-off Canadians. There is a more fair and appropriate way to do it. The Government has chosen not to put people first. We need only look at the United States and the United Kingdom to see the price paid by ordinary people there, governments to which this Government pays so much attention. We can see it at work in Canada, too. The gap between the rich and the poor is getting larger. Four million Canadians live at or below the poverty line, and children in large numbers go to bed hungry. This Government must not close its eyes to this situation. Rhetoric on the part of the Government is not enough. Governments have an obligation and a duty to address the concerns of those less well off in society, and Canadians who are less well off have a right to have their concerns addressed. Instead, this Government does what the privileged, the wealthy, and the corporate establishment wants. It responds to their concerns, not to the concerns of ordinary Canadians. The Throne Speech makes that quite clear.
This Government has reneged on its pre-election statements and has reneged on its obligations to less well off Canadians. Cut-backs in health and post-secondary education funding to the provinces will take place in the Budget of April 27. This is not only short-sighted, but it poses difficulties and is painful to those less well off Canadians who cannot afford health care and education on their own.
Canadians are our most important resource, and to reduce contributions to the provinces which will reduce expenditures in our health and post-secondary education systems is folly at best. Indeed, this Government's policy on these matters fails even within its own sense of priority in economic terms. An investment in the future in healthy and well educated Canadians can only bring returns.
The people of Saskatoon-Clark's Crossing defeated a senior and well respected cabinet Minister of the previous Government. He was not defeated because he was a bad MR He was defeated because the policies of his Party did not represent what the people of Saskatoon- Clark's Crossing thought were important. They did not represent a people first ideology.

April 12, 1989
The Address-Mr. Axworthy
The people of Saskatoon-Clark's Crossing voted against free trade. They were worried that the deal would result in fewer jobs in Canada. They were mocked by the Prime Minister and told that they did not understand what was happening. They were worried about threats to social programs and about the system of supply management which protects Saskatchewan farm families. The Prime Minister promised that all these would be untouched. Yet in the last few weeks, indeed yesterday, we have seen major attacks on social programs and on the Wheat Board. We have seen many job losses over the last short while. The Government says one thing and it does another.
In addition, we have seen a great disappointment with the Throne Speech among not only Saskatchewan farm families but other Canadian farm families too. As the amendment of the Official Opposition indicates, totally inadequate consideration was given to the problems of agriculture in this country.
In 1985 the Minister of Agriculture, after an ad hoc drought program that year which seemed not to be satisfactory, promised a permanent program in the future so that farmers would know where they stood financially. Yet we still have not seen it.
In the last election, the New Democratic Party's family farm protection policy put forward a strategy which could ensure that farmers would know where they stood from year to year and would know, when they planted their crop, what they could expect to receive from it. We argued strongly for strengthening farm marketing boards and supply management, for fairer alternatives to farm debt and for more tax fairness for farmers. We encouraged farm soil and water conservation policies. We argued to reduce the input costs experienced by farmers, and we argued for better commodity handling and transportation.
The Throne Speech makes no mention of addressing these problems, and I would like to move an amendment to the amendment which is presently on the floor, seconded by the Hon. Member for New Westminster- Burnaby (Ms. Black). It adds two items to the amendment and reads as follows:
(7)	by yet again ignoring the need for permanent crop disaster program as promised in December of 1985; and
(8)	by ignoring the needs of rural communities for basic income security and the refusal to provide a Family Farm Stabilization Program.

Mr. Speaker, I have a brief comment. As I was listening to the Hon. Member across the way stating that the Conservative Government had created a national debt, I would just like to make it clear on the record that in 1984 the previous Government left us with an annual deficit of some $38 billion. I do believe that it does not take a rocket scientist to realize that in the operation of the administration of this country that two factors come into play. One is our cumulative national deficit and our annual national debt.
In 1984, if my memory serves me correctly, I believe the national debt was approximately $190 billion, with an annual deficit in 1983-84 of some $38 billion. I would assume that if the Opposition had stayed in power our annual deficit would have sky-rocketed to more than $38 billion.
If we add four years times $40 billion, being very conservative to the Opposition, we arrive without servicing our cumulative debt at over $350 billion. If my memory serves me right, in 1985 the Opposition, after the economic statement of our great Minister of Finance, predicted that there would be in excess of over 200,000 jobs.
We know that just the opposite is true. There have been over a million jobs created by this Government in four short years. I would like to impress upon the Official Opposition and the NDP that the Conservatives did not create our national debt. If the Official Opposition had stayed in power, we would not be going into the year 2000; we would be running away from it.

What I have been trying to argue for, and what the Opposition and the New Democratic Party have continually argued for, is that if we are going to attack this deficit let us at least do it fairly. Let us be sure that corporations pay their fair share of taxes. Let us at least make sure that those 60,000 Canadians who do not pay any taxes pay their fair share.
Surely we cannot accept as a proper way of taxing Canadians that we tax those whose total income for the year is below the poverty line. The poverty line for a single person living in a Canadian city is around $11,000. We start taxing those people at $6,000, while we let Canadians earning over $50,000 pay no tax at all.

speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
