speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to take part in the debate ont the Speech from the Throne, and I will certainly have a few things to say to the dreamers who were telling us how to reduce the deficit.
After listening to speeches by several Members of the Opposition, our socialist dreamers and our Liberal friends, I think that at this stage, Mr. Speaker, we should remember that by re-electing our Government on November 21, Canadian voters indicated that they agreed with the way we as a Government had managed Canada during the previous four years. They were satisfied with our responsible approach to the economy and to how that economy should be managed, and I think they were also pleased with steps taken by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney), by the Government and the House of Commons regarding our plans for national reconciliation.
By re-electing our Gouvernment on November 21, Canadians expressed their approval of the plans for the future proposed by the Prime Minister and the Government, plans based on a continuum that will lead to a stronger economy, a more caring society and a more united Canada. This vision of the future, Mr. Speaker, was based on the conviction held by Members of our
The Address-Mr Valcourt
Party that Canadians have the talent, energy and determination to face the future with confidence, confident in our identity as Canadians, our values and our culture.
As for the Opposition Parties, we all know what they promised Canadian voters! What the Liberal Party had to offer and it did have something to offer-was fear, withdrawal, and a desire to go back to times long since past. Canadians simply said no to all that. Canadians said no, and despite the fact that the Liberals perpetreated acts of intellectual terrorism across the country, despite the fact that they again wanted to tell Canadians the country did not have what it takes to face the future, Canadians said: No thanks. Canadians are people who have confidence in their own capabilities, but the Leader of the Liberal Party still rises in the House to say that Canadians made a mistake. He will not respect the will of the people! I heard him say last week it was our friends in the business world, Mr. Speaker, who helped us win the election. Lor a gentleman who spent almost ten years on Bay Street, I think he is rather quick to repudiate his friends. Unless it was the other way round, and his friends repudiated him!
The fact is, Mr. Speaker, and this is something the Opposition refuses to admit, that since 1984, we have been the Government of all Canadians, and that is why we were re-elected on November 21.
We are now starting on our second mandate in the same spirit with which we approached our first, with a renewed desire to stimulate economic growth and regional development, and a constant concern for social justice and equal opportunities in our regions.

I have listened closely in the last few days to the statements made by opposition Members in this House. To hear them speak, it is as if the Speech from the Throne were only about reducing the deficit. That is all they take from the Speech from the Throne. However, anyone who cares to read it to see what the Government has proposed will know that it is a plan for the next four years for the benefit of Canadians from all regions of Canada.
These people prefer to ignore the fact that reducing the deficit is not an end in itself but is, rather, an essential condition for achieving our objectives. These objectives are laid out in the Speech from the Throne. If we have to talk about the deficit today, it is because of

April 12, 1989
The Address-Mr. Valcourt
the army of Santa Clauses on the other side of the Elouse from an earlier Government.
I have heard many complaints from the two Parties in the Opposition. They were sorry that there was not a long list of promises in the Speech from the Throne. We have not said we would be everything to everyone. Rather, we have placed before Canadians a plan and objectives for what I suspect all Canadians want to maintain, that is, to ensure that in the future our kids can also benefit from the rich country that Canada is.
We are a trading nation. We are an exporting nation. The opening up of new markets will bring exceptional opportunities, provided that our economy is competitive and flexible. We intend to take the necessary steps to ensure that our industries and businesses adapt rapidly to the new market conditions. For example, it is proposed in the Speech from the Throne that we will assist small and medium sized businesses that wish to enter new export markets.
In this more open economy assistance to business will also involve two key activities-technological development and human resources development. This means that literacy training, occupational retraining and education are the keys for a workforce that is better qualified for higher quality jobs. These are also the conditions needed to penetrate an increasingly competitive marketplace effectively.
I think these objectives mean spending public funds in a way that returns dividends to society as a whole. That is what I think Canadians expect of us.

Mr. Speaker, last fall we asked Canadians to say yes to an exciting challenge. We did so because we knew that our fellow citizens do not have cold feet. They have confidence. They have the talent to do better what others do well. What the Speech from the Throne offers them today is to provide this great plan of freer trade, not only with the United States but also with other countries in the world, with the best chance of success. At the same time, the Government will continue to fight regional disparities.
Mr. Speaker, I am glad that the Speech from the Throne announces that funding will be maintained for economic development agencies such as ACOA in Atlantic Canada, FEDNOR in northern Ontario and the Western Economic Diversification Office.
We will also continue to help those in greatest need: our seniors, our low income people, our youth, and especially those who are victims of family violence.

Building a prosperous economy, maintaining our social programs and developing our regions in a harmonious way must be accompanied by a strengthening of Canadian unity.
Nearly two years ago, the Prime Minister of Canada and the 10 provincial Premiers signed an historic agreement, an agreement which returned Quebec to the constitutional fold, which recognized its status as a distinct society within Canada and which committed the country's leaders to protecting Canada's linguistic minorities.
As a Canadian and as an Acadian from New Brunswick, I am delighted by the signing of the Meech Lake Accord. For reasons of their own the Premiers of Manitoba and New Brunswick have not felt themselves bound by the commitment of their predecessors. As a citizen of New Brunswick and a Francophone from that province, I regret the hesitation of provincial authorities in ratifying the Accord. No one on this side of the Elouse has ever claimed that the Meech Lake Accord is perfect. We are saying that it is an essential basis on which Canadians will build their constitutional future.
In a brief that I presented to the special committee of the Legislative Assembly of New Brunswick, I said: "There is not one provision in this Accord which can put in jeopardy the rights of, or cause a backward step for, any group whether it be linguistic minority, women or native".
The Meech Lake Accord is a monument of balance and realism accomplished at the price of long and hard negotiation. It would be irresponsible to jeopardize it by opening new negotiations. If we took this route, we would be opening Pandora's box and heading for a new constitutional crisis that could drag on for a very long time. As Canadians concerned for the unity of our country, we cannot allow this to happen.
New Brunswick has always played an active role in the constitutional development of Canada. Two great Premiers, Messrs. Robichaud and Hatfield, have been leaders in promoting both official languages and the equality of their communities. In ratifying the Meech Lake Accord, Premier McKenna would be joining this great tradition of fairness and generosity in New Brunswick. He would be fulfilling the wishes of Acadians and


April 12, 1989

Francophones in his Province of New Brunswick. After the passage of Bill C-72 last year, the language communities would have available, with Meech, another instrument to serve their rights.

Of course, the Accord is not a constitutional panacea. The Government admits this in the Speech from the Throne by promising, once the Accord is ratified, to proceed with negotiations on Senate reform, aboriginal rights, fisheries roles and responsibilities and the language issue.
This is much more than politics, Mr. Speaker. It is the very future of the country, its balance, its ability to respond to changes, to meet requirements of flexibility and modernity.
The Canada of the Meech Lake Accord corresponds to reality and is not just a mental concept. It is made up of different people united by a common attachment to their country and inspired by a common feeling of fairness, tolerance and sharing. This vision of Canada must be written into the country's Constitution as quickly as possible.
Another challenge faced by Canadans is the environment. I am deeply satisfied that in the Throne Speech this Government put forward a plan to ensure that we will leave our children and their children a healthy-environmental heritage. Steps are put forward in the Throne Speech to ensure that our environment is protected, not by lip service but rather by taking action, implementing programs. It is my belief Canadians will welcome that initiative taken by this Government.
Another item in the Throne Speech involves social programs. Of course when we are working at creating wealth, at meeting social needs, protecting the quality of life, this as I said earlier is something we are doing for the benefit of future generations, because they must not have to shoulder the burden of our neglect.
And this is what is involved also when we speak today of reducing the deficit and the national debt.
We were famous over these last four years, Mr. Speaker, for being the first Government in decades with a serious commitment to tackle the deficit. I remember hearing in this House the Leader of the Opposition and the leader of those dreamers the necktie socialists tell
The Address-Mr. Valcourt
Canadians our budget reductions in 1984 were going to lose hundreds of thousands of jobs in Canada.
The result is that 1.4 million jobs were created during those four years. And again we will hear the same prophets of doom after the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) has delivered his Budget speech. However Canadians have already seen the positive results of our sound financial administration.
Mr. Speaker, I see that you are about to interrupt me. It is unfortunate that time be so short, but I am sure the Budget speech will provide us with a number of opportunities to respond to those who dream about bringing the deficit down and would have Canadians believe that a mere 60 taxpayers is all we need to reduce the deficit by $30 billion!

Mr. Nun/.iata: I want to ask the Hon. Member about an important issue facing our country, one that was given only a cursory glance in the Throne Speech. It is a problem that is destroying the very fabric of our nation and our youth. It will continue to destroy many young people in Canada. The problem is that of drug abuse.
I have concerns regarding the priorities of this Government and how it intends to deal with this issue. It was important for the Government to hold a royal commission of inquiry into drug abuse in amateur sport. We are all concerned about that, but that problem pales in comparison to the real drug problem in Canada. I am sure there is a problem in the Minister's own riding when it comes to drug abuse.
We in Canada have been fortunate that the drug problem is not as bad as it is in the United States. I had a conversation with several crown attorneys last week. They expressed serious concerns about the crack problem in Canada. They indicated that in three to five years our drug problems will be comparable to those in the United States. We are all familiar with the problem of crack, a derivative of cocaine. It creates violence. The City of Washington in the United States now holds the record for the most number of drug related deaths.
I would like to ask the Minister what the Government intends to do about this serious problem. Will he recommend to his cabinet colleagues and the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) that there be a royal commission of inquiry into the drug abuse problem in Canada?

April 12, 1989
The Address-Mr. Valcourt
Will he urge his colleagues in Cabinet to give this problem the priority it deserves? In the Throne Speech a few days ago, this problem was not given the prominence it deserves. May I hear from the Minister?
